taskContent:
Two homogeneous materials are available for an insert in a workshop. A completely filled sample of each material is considered. The following model values each refer to the same entire sample; the volumes are already given and need not be calculated geometrically.

| Sample | Mass | Volume |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| A | 450 g | 0.180 L |
| B | 520 g | 260 cm³ |

1. Determine the density of both materials in a suitable common unit of your choice. Construct your approach from mass and volume, perform the necessary unit conversion, and document your calculations. (3 marks)
2. Explain for each material what your density value means as **mass per unit volume**, for example for 1 cm³ or 1 L. A formula with a unit alone is insufficient as an interpretation. Also explain what happens to the mass, volume and density when exactly half of sample A is taken. (3 marks)
3. Justify which material has the greater density even though sample B has the greater total mass. The insert requires exactly 80 cm³ of one material: calculate the required mass for each material and justify which material has the smaller mass at that same volume. (3 marks)

Mathematically equivalent approaches, such as ratio reasoning or unitary methods, are acceptable; no particular formula notation or calculator model is prescribed. An explained, labelled representation may replace a verbal explanation if it clearly shows the same meaning. The ordinary pass threshold is at least 7 of 9 marks. There is no further passing tier.
solutionContent:
One possible common reference is grams per cubic centimetre. Here 0.180 L = 180 cm³. Density is mass divided by its corresponding volume: ρ = m/V. Thus A has 450 g / 180 cm³ = 2.5 g/cm³ and B has 520 g / 260 cm³ = 2.0 g/cm³.

This means that 1 cm³ of material A has a mass of 2.5 g, while 1 cm³ of material B has a mass of 2.0 g. Equivalently, 1 L may be interpreted as having mass 2.5 kg for A and 2.0 kg for B. Merely repeating the quotient or the unit is not yet an explicit explanation of its meaning. Halving the homogeneous sample A halves both its mass and volume: 225 g and 90 cm³. Density remains 225 g / 90 cm³ = 2.5 g/cm³ because both quantities change by the same factor.

Material A is denser: it has more mass at the same volume. The greater total mass of the entire sample B does not prove greater density because B also has a greater volume. At 80 cm³, A requires 2.5 g/cm³ · 80 cm³ = 200 g, while B requires 2.0 g/cm³ · 80 cm³ = 160 g. B therefore has 40 g less mass at the same required volume.

Other consistent units, for example 2.5 and 2.0 kg/L or 2500 and 2000 kg/m³, are also valid, as are unitary reasoning, a ratio/correspondence table or an unambiguous labelled representation. Every approach must show the mass-per-volume meaning, the units used and the concrete application. The stated volumes are data; prism formulas and surface-area calculations are not part of this assessment.
